title: Case study: unique ID generator
objective: Make unique IDs on many machines at once, with no central counter: pack the time, the machine number and a small counter into one number that sorts by time.

sources.title: Twitter's Snowflake README (2010 release): 41 bits of milliseconds, 10-bit machine id, 12-bit sequence; machines don't coordinate; refuses to make IDs if the clock goes backwards

simplifies: The trace uses a tiny layout (2 machine bits and 2 sequence bits) so the numbers stay readable; Twitter's published Snowflake uses 41 bits of time, 10 of machine and 12 of sequence. In the trace a machine whose counter is full moves on to the next millisecond; Snowflake's README says it refuses to make IDs while its clock is behind the last time it used.

critique.prompt: A proposal: every service gets new IDs from one database counter; each ID machine picks its machine number at random when it starts; if the clock is moved back, machines carry on with whatever time it says.

risks.text: One counter database is a single point of failure: when it's down, nothing can be created
risks.why: Generate IDs on each machine from time, machine number and a sequence.

risks.text: Random machine numbers can collide, and two machines with the same number make the same IDs
risks.why: Assign machine numbers so each is unique (from configuration or a coordination service).

risks.text: Carrying on after the clock moves back can repeat IDs already handed out
risks.why: Do what Snowflake's README describes: refuse to make IDs until the clock passes the last time used.
That's what Snowflake aims for: compact and fast to compare.

risks.text: IDs sort roughly by creation time
risks.why: That's a feature: newest-first lists can sort by ID.

critique.hint: Think about one machine going down, two machines picking the same number, and a clock being corrected.

first.prompt: Every service stops creating orders whenever one database restarts. Which fix comes first?

options.text: Stop using one central counter: make IDs on each machine
options.explanation: Right. That's the risk that stops everything at once.

options.text: Assign machine numbers instead of picking them at random
options.explanation: Important, but it causes rare duplicates, not a full stop.

options.text: Refuse to make IDs while the clock is behind
options.explanation: Also important, but clocks moving back is occasional.

critique.explain: Remove the single point of failure first; then make sure no two machines share a number, and never hand out IDs from a clock that went backwards.

quiz.prompt: Why does each ID include the machine number?

options.text: Two machines making an ID in the same millisecond still get different IDs, without asking each other
options.explanation: Right. That's what removes the need for a central counter.

options.text: To know which machine to blame for bugs
options.explanation: Handy, but uniqueness is the reason.
Length isn't the goal; uniqueness without coordination is.

quiz.prompt: Why put the time in the highest bits?

options.text: Then sorting IDs as numbers sorts them by when they were made
options.explanation: Right. Newest-first is just "largest ID first".

options.text: Time is the most important number
options.explanation: It's about sort order, not importance.
The machine number and sequence make them unique; the time's position makes them sortable.
